When political combatants weaponize falling national crime data to attack mainstream media and political rivals, public safety becomes a partisan football.
Evidence: Selective crime stats, media omission claims, partisan attribution
#Aletheia #USPol

The Federalist claims that felony violent crime plunged 25% in 2025 solely due to Trump administration policies, while major media outlets hypocritically ignored the data. 🌐
Stated Judgement: (+1.00, +1.00) — Greater Good

While federal data shows downward crime trends continuing across multiple jurisdictions (including states like California), the article frames complex post-pandemic shifts into a partisan wedge.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.80, -0.90) — Greater Evil

Verdict: FAIL — Fall into Destruction.
Partisan narrative framing exploits genuine crime declines to manufacture systemic media villainy and partisan purity tests.

Integrity: Severe Deception (Hypocrisy: 12.80, z: 4)

- The Federalist: FAIL (-0.8, -0.9) — Selective attribution of national crime trends.
- Crime Statistics: COND (0.0, 0.0) — Real BJS data framed with partisan spin.
The debate centers on Bureau of Justice Statistics data showing a 25% drop in felony violent crime in 2025, triggering fierce battles over credit and media transparency ahead of elections.

The Poison:
Weaponizing real improvements in public safety to drive tribal polarization, framing routine editorial news choices as active treasonous coverups.

Plane Error:
Confusing empirical statistical trends (WHAT) with partisan media conspiracy accusations (WHO). The article substitutes institutional data analysis for political blame.

Social Physics Analysis:
The publication runs a Smart Selfish Maneuver by taking verified positive societal outcomes, attaching them exclusively to political allies, and manufacturing a hostile media enemy.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall into Destruction.
Modal Dynamics: can be -> is not via Red Top (The Imperial Trap).
Promising inclusive safety potential is inverted into exclusive partisan erasure.

The Unavoidable Truth: Felony violent crime rates dropped significantly in 2025 across the United States.

The Unavoidable Lie: Major media silence on this single BJS report proves a coordinated partisan cover-up.

Alethekanon:
Subsuming objective empirical progress under partisan grievance transforms public data into a sectarian weapon, destroying shared reality for tribal advantage.

Awwthekanon:
Communities healing from crime deserve honest, steady support, not bitter political point-scoring that treats human safety as a weapon to bludgeon opponents.

Brothekanon:
Crime going down is objectively awesome news for everyone, so turning it into a massive media conspiracy fight feels exhausting and totally unnecessary.

Spirithekanon:
"Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin condemns any people." Proverbs 14:34 PASS
Truth and safety should be cherished as shared blessings rather than distorted into weapons of division.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
The Media Won’t Tell You Felony Violent Crime Is Plunging Under Trump

The reasons behind these record crime reductions aren't difficult to understand.

Actual Article Body:
The reasons behind these record crime reductions aren’t difficult to understand.

Most people who follow the news probably missed Monday’s announcement from the Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS): Felony violent crime plunged 25 percent in 2025. Rape fell 13 percent, robbery dropped 27 percent, and aggravated assault declined 31 percent. Property crime fell 19 percent. Except for rape, these represent the largest one-year declines since the government began collecting these data 53 years ago.

That marks a dramatic reversal from the Biden administration, when felony violent crime soared by a record 59 percent and property crime rose 8 percent between 2021 and 2024.

Murders also plummeted. The U.S. recorded approximately 4.1 murders per 100,000 people in 2025, a record low, down from 5.1 in 2024. The murder rate has continued to fall. If the additional 18.4 percent decline shown in preliminary FBI data for the first seven months of 2026 holds for the full year, the murder rate would drop to approximately 3.36 per 100,000.

You might expect these unprecedented declines in violent and property crime and record low crime rates to dominate the news. Instead, most major media outlets ignored Monday’s announcement. While the New York Post and CBS covered the new data, the Associated Press, Reuters, CNN, NBC News, ABC News, the New York Times, and the Washington Post apparently didn’t consider the historic reductions newsworthy.

That lack of coverage is particularly surprising because new October polls show that voters still care about crime. A Pew Research Center poll found that 52 percent of registered voters consider violent crime a “very important” issue, while an AP-NORC survey found that 45 percent of adults identify immigration and crime as top issues.

The reasons behind these record crime reductions aren’t difficult to understand. FBI arrests soared 184 percent in 2025 compared with 2024, U.S. attorneys across the country stepped up criminal prosecutions, and the Trump administration federalized law enforcement in Washington, D.C., and Memphis. In D.C., the Biden administration’s U.S. attorney charged only about 33 percent of those arrested. Under Trump, that rate jumped to 96 percent.

Nor is it a coincidence that crime had record percent increases during the Biden administration as record numbers of illegal immigrants entered the country and is now plummeting as the Trump administration seals the border and deports illegal immigrants. The Department of Homeland Security says approximately 70 percent of illegal immigrants deported under the Trump administration had criminal convictions or pending criminal charges.

Even illegal immigrants who have committed crimes but haven’t been caught have an incentive to avoid deportation. By stopping their criminal activity, they can stay off the police radar and reduce their risk of being deported.

At the end of 2025, New York incarcerated 7,113 illegal immigrants, representing 14 percent of the state’s inmate population — at least 3.4 times their share of the state’s population.

But Democrats are promising to reverse these policies. Some Democrats, including New York congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier, advocate abolishing prisons. Others, from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to Pete Buttigieg to Sen. Bernie Sanders, want to cut the prison population in half.

In Congress, 61 House Democrats voted against a resolution condemning calls to “defund the police.” Another 57 House Democrats support completely rescinding the ICE funding provided in last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries has promised that if Democrats regain control of Congress, they will work to bring back illegal immigrants whom the Trump administration has already deported. Meanwhile, just 15 House Democrats were willing to sign a letter declaring, “We want safety, not lawlessness.”

Americans who thought the last two years’ government shutdowns were long — the 43-day shutdown in 2025 and the 76-day partial shutdown earlier this year — may face an even longer confrontation. Democrats’ push to defund ICE will almost certainly trigger a Trump veto, setting up a massive train wreck between two sides firmly entrenched in their positions.

Democrats claim to champion the poor and minorities, yet those are precisely the people who suffer most from crime. Criminals overwhelmingly victimize people in their own communities, often striking close to where they live. And the damage extends far beyond the immediate victims. Who loses their jobs when crime forces neighborhood stores to close? Who loses access to affordable shopping? Who owns homes whose property values are depressed because of the crime?

The divide between Democrats and Republicans over crime could hardly be sharper, and the elections next week will determine if these record drops in crime will continue. Republicans emphasize arrests, prosecutions, incarceration, and deportations, while Democrats increasingly advocate reducing incarceration and limiting traditional law enforcement and immigration enforcement.
